current.lab_name: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University (Guangzhou, China)

story: Myopia (short-sightedness) usually happens because the eyeball grows too long. The sclera, the tough white outer wall of the eye, has to remodel for that to happen. Xiaoxiao Zhang was senior author of the 2026 FASEB Journal study in this Atlas (WEN2026), which used human scleral cells and guinea pigs whose eyes were covered to induce myopia. Too much autophagy in the sclera, the cell's recycling system, appeared to link low-oxygen stress to the remodelling. Rapamycin injected under the conjunctiva made the myopia worse, the autophagy blocker 3-MA eased it, and atropine eye drops slowed it. The team measured AMPK/mTOR/P70S6K signalling, but the paper does not show that this route causes the effect, and the results come from cells and animals, not children.

A companion 2026 paper from the same Guangzhou group, again with Zhang as last author, traced the low-oxygen signal one step further: in hypoxic scleral cells and in guinea pigs, the HIF-1alpha protein pushed cells towards glycolysis and lactate production, and blocking glycolysis reduced myopic eye growth.

Much of Zhang's other published work is clinical. PubMed lists papers from Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital on a vision screening of more than 170,000 primary school pupils in three Guangzhou districts (2025), on predicting eye growth in children wearing orthokeratology night lenses over six years (2025), on comparing two kinds of myopia-control spectacle lenses (2023), and on eyelid hygiene during orthokeratology (2026). The hospital is affiliated with Jinan University.

studies.title: Role of Autophagy in Scleral Remodeling During Form-Deprivation Myopia

current.lab_name: Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
current.role: Immunologist at Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou whose group showed in mice that losing the lysosomal mTOR-activating protein Lamtor5 with age pushes macrophages into senescence and spreads inflammation
current.sub: Key Laboratory of Artificial Organs and Computational Medicine, Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (papers 2024–2026)
story: Liyun Shi is senior author of an Atlas study (LV2026) on why the immune system ages. Lamtor5 is one of the five small proteins of the Ragulator complex, the platform on the lysosome surface where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. The team found that Lamtor5 levels fall with age in mouse macrophages, the immune cells that clean up debris and fight infection. Without enough Lamtor5 the macrophages became senescent, a state in which cells stop dividing but release inflammatory signals. The study traced this to the cGAS-STING pathway, an alarm system that senses DNA in the wrong place in the cell, and showed that the inflammation spread to other tissues. Restoring Lamtor5 in old mice reduced these signs of immune ageing.

The finding links a component of the mTOR machinery to inflammaging, the low-level chronic inflammation of old age. It is a mouse study, so whether Lamtor5 behaves the same way in human immune cells remains open.

PubMed lists Shi at the Institute of Translational Medicine of Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou on the Atlas paper and on a 2024 study, with clinical partners, of how gut bacteria and a population of macrophages drive bowel inflammation in children with glycogen storage disease type Ib. No official profile page was found, so the exact current title is not confirmed.

studies.title: Age-associated decline of Lamtor5 drives immunosenescence and systemic aging via cGAS-mediated paracrine inflammation.

current.role: Senior author of the 2021 report of resTORbio's phase 2b and phase 3 trials of the mTOR inhibitor RTB101 to protect older adults from respiratory infections
current.sub: resTORbio, Boston (PubMed affiliation, 2021, at the time of the study) · current position not confirmed
story: The immune system weakens with age, and the idea tested here was that blocking mTOR could improve immune function in older adults. MAN2021, published in Lancet Healthy Longevity in 2021 with Sarb Shergill as last author and the authors listed at resTORbio, reports two large tests of that idea with RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, taken once a day for 16 weeks by adults aged 65 and over.

In the phase 2b trial (652 people), fewer people on 10 mg had a laboratory-confirmed respiratory infection than on placebo (19% against 28%), but this came from a pooled analysis not corrected for multiple testing, and the corrected analysis was not significant. The phase 3 trial (1,024 people) used a different main endpoint agreed with the FDA, illness with or without a lab test, and found no difference (26% against 25%). Blood tests in both trials still showed more antiviral genes switched on. For readers, the lesson is that a promising biological signal in older people did not turn into fewer illnesses in the larger trial.
PubMed lists only this paper for Sarb Shergill, with the affiliation resTORbio, Boston. No official biography was found, so the role at the company and the current position could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials

current.sub: Principal investigator, School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, Hangzhou (papers to 2026) · Media Lab, MIT (Edward Boyden lab, papers around 2018) · Department of Anatomy and Structural Biology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Vladislav Verkhusha lab, papers 2009–2014)
story: Most ways of measuring mTOR activity give a snapshot: you break open the cells at one moment and look. In the Atlas study WANG2026C, Piatkevich's lab built a fluorescent protein ticker tape, a set of self-assembling protein fibres that grow inside a cell and lay down fluorescent colour bands over time, like rings in a tree trunk. Each colour can be tied to the activity of a different signalling pathway, including mTOR, NF-kB, STAT3, NFAT and cAMP. Reading the bands later gives a history of each pathway in each single cell, in culture and in living animals.

Using the mTOR version, the team saw mTOR activity rise and fall in step with the cell division cycle. That supports the idea that mTOR signalling is dynamic, not a fixed on or off state, which is one of the Atlas's current themes. The recording was done in cells and animals, not in people.

On PubMed, Piatkevich's first papers (from 2009) come from Vladislav Verkhusha's lab at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York, on fluorescent timers that change colour as proteins age and on red fluorescent proteins with unusual colour properties. By 2018 the papers come from Edward Boyden's group at the MIT Media Lab, including Archon1, a fluorescent voltage reporter for imaging electrical activity in neurons, found with a robotic cell-picking screen. Recent papers come from Piatkevich's own group at the School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, in Hangzhou, on far-red fluorescent proteins and super-resolution imaging, and the Atlas paper also lists Zhejiang University.

studies.title: Fluorescent protein ticker tape (FPTT): Multiplexed recording of transcriptional dynamics in living cells and in vivo

story: In DAB2026, Malgorzata Firczuk's group in Warsaw asked whether blocking mTORC1, the growth-control complex, could help antibody drugs that target CD20, a protein on the surface of B cells. In B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, CD20 is often low. The team found that mTORC1 inhibitors raise CD20 through AKT and the transcription factor FOXO1 and push the leukemia cells towards a more mature B-cell state, which made anti-CD20 antibodies work better, including in high-risk disease with IKZF1 deletions. This is preclinical work that supports testing the combination; it does not show benefit in patients.

Firczuk works at the Department of Immunology of the Medical University of Warsaw and the Laboratory of Immunology of the Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences, and has about two dozen PubMed papers on leukemia and lymphoma. A recurring theme is how leukemia cells handle oxidative stress. In 2024, as senior author, Firczuk reported that the antioxidant enzyme peroxiredoxin-1 is high in Philadelphia-positive B-ALL, and that blocking the thioredoxin system together with a DNA repair route called non-homologous end joining makes these cells much more sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

story: Fengjing Guo is the senior author of a 2026 review, led by Jingting Xu, on mTORC2, the less studied of the two mTOR complexes, and its essential partner RICTOR. mTORC2 passes its signals through the kinases AKT, SGK1 and PKC, and the review follows these signals through T cells, B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells and natural killer cells.

story: Gianluca Figlia appears on two Atlas studies about brakes on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2021 Cell paper (PRE2021) found that G3BP1 and G3BP2, proteins best known from stress granules, also sit on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment where mTORC1 is switched on. There they hold the TSC complex, the main off-switch for mTORC1, in place. Without them mTORC1 reacts too strongly to amino acids and insulin. The 2023 Nature Cell Biology paper (NIC2023) showed that malonyl-CoA, a building block made on the way to new fatty acids, fits into the same pocket of mTOR that normally holds ATP and so blocks it. When a cell cannot make fat fast enough, malonyl-CoA rises and slows mTORC1 down. Both results come mainly from cells; the first adds zebrafish experiments, and the second shows the malonyl-CoA effect is conserved across species.

Figlia's path ran through two labs that both linked mTOR to lipids. At ETH Zurich, in Ueli Suter's group, Figlia was second author of a 2014 Cell Reports paper showing in mice that mTORC1 in Schwann cells, the cells that wrap nerves in insulating myelin, drives myelin growth by switching on fat-making genes through SREBP. At the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, in Aurelio Teleman's group, Figlia was first author of a 2020 review on how metabolites control signalling by attaching chemically to proteins, and first author of a 2025 EMBO Journal paper showing that cells sense glutamine for mTORC1 entirely through the kinase GCN2, triggered by the loss of asparagine.
The 2025 paper and a 2026 commentary on TDP-43 disease list Figlia at the Institute of Neuropathology, RWTH Aachen University Hospital.

story: Julie St-Pierre is a co-author on two Atlas studies from McGill University about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and energy metabolism. The 2013 Cell Metabolism paper (MOR2013), led by Nahum Sonenberg's group, showed in cells that mTORC1 sets how many mitochondria a cell builds and how hard they work. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations. mTORC1 does this by releasing the brake that 4E-BP proteins put on the production of proteins the mitochondria need. This links the growth signal directly to the energy supply that growth needs.

The 2026 Journal of Endocrinology paper (BCH2026), from Vincent Giguère's group, is a mouse study. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, can cause fatty liver, and adding the antimalarial drug chloroquine made that fatty liver milder. The rescue depended on ERR-alpha, a nuclear receptor that switches on many energy metabolism genes; in mice without it, chloroquine did not help.

St-Pierre worked for many years at McGill's Goodman Cancer Research Centre and Department of Biochemistry, where in 2018 St-Pierre was also a co-author on the study of how ERR-alpha shapes fatty liver on a high-fat diet. The 2026 paper lists St-Pierre at both the Goodman Cancer Institute and the University of Ottawa, in the Ottawa Institute of Systems Biology and the Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology.

story: Ines Deleu is a co-author of the two Atlas reports from BOLERO-2, a large trial in postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer that is driven by hormones (hormone-receptor-positive) and does not carry extra copies of the HER2 gene. These cancers often learn to grow despite hormone treatment, and switching on the mTOR pathway is one way they do it. BOLERO-2 added everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to the hormone drug exemestane. The first report (BAS2012) showed that the combination kept the cancer from growing for several months longer than exemestane alone. The final report (PIC2014) found that this gain held up, but that overall survival was not significantly longer (31.0 against 26.6 months).

Large cancer trials like this one run at hundreds of hospitals, and site investigators enrol and treat the patients, collect the data and sign off on the final paper. PubMed lists Deleu at AZ Nikolaas, a general hospital in Sint-Niklaas in Flanders, on about a dozen papers, most of them multicentre breast cancer trials. The most recent, from 2022, is the phase III EMERALD trial of elacestrant, an oral drug that breaks down the estrogen receptor.

story: Julie Mattison was first author of the 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that compared the two long-term studies of calorie restriction in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin. Eating less without malnutrition extends life in many animals, and lower mTOR activity is one of the routes thought to explain it. The two monkey studies had reached different conclusions about survival. Looking at both data sets together, the authors found consistent health benefits, while the survival effect depended on study design and on the diet of the control animals. This is evidence from monkeys, not from people.

Mattison was also first author of the 2012 Nature paper reporting that calorie restriction had not improved survival in the NIA monkeys, at that time listed at the Laboratory of Experimental Gerontology at the NIH Animal Center in Dickerson, Maryland, with Rafael de Cabo as senior author. That result, at odds with the Wisconsin study, set up the 2017 comparison.

In the Atlas, Mattison is also a co-author of a 2021 study (HOR2021) that built epigenetic clocks for the common marmoset, a small monkey, and found that rapamycin did not significantly change epigenetic age in these animals. PubMed lists Mattison at the NIA Translational Gerontology Branch on more recent papers, including a 2026 preprint on muscle aging that used cells from old and young rhesus monkeys.

story: Emma Baar is a co-author of two linked mouse studies from Dudley Lamming's lab in this Atlas (ARR2015, ARR2016). Rapamycin is the best-tested drug for extending lifespan in mice, but given every day it causes side effects such as poor blood sugar control and weaker immune responses. In ARR2015, mice given rapamycin daily (2 mg/kg) became glucose intolerant and their insulin-producing islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every five days left glucose and insulin tolerance normal, while dosing every three days was already too frequent. In ARR2016, female mice that started the every-five-days schedule at 20 months of age, which is old for a mouse, lived longer than untreated females. Taken together, the two mouse studies suggest that rapamycin's lifespan benefit can be partly separated from its side effects by giving it intermittently. This conclusion comes from combining two experiments in mice, not from a single study, and has not been tested this way in people.

Baar was first author of a 2015 Aging Cell paper that measured mTOR signalling in several tissues of male and female mice at different ages and found that the changes with age differ by sex and by tissue. As a member of the Lamming group, Baar also co-authored work showing that losing Rictor, a core part of the second mTOR complex mTORC2, shortens the life of male mice (2014), that eating fewer branched-chain amino acids improves metabolic health (2016), that a new rapamycin-like drug can block mTORC1 selectively in animals (2019), and that the better insulin sensitivity seen with calorie restriction depends on mTORC2 in fat tissue (2019).
The most recent paper in PubMed with Baar's name is from 2020. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: Chun-Yan Lim is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited to the lysosome. SHI2022 identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein previously known only as GPR155, as a cholesterol sensor for mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Cholesterol binds one end of LYCHOS, and mutating that site weakens mTORC1 activation. When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that normally keeps mTORC1 off, and so lets mTORC1 be recruited to the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. The work was done in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Lim's own Berkeley work tied these pieces to disease. As first author of a 2019 Nature Cell Biology paper, Lim showed that contact points between the endoplasmic reticulum and the lysosome let mTORC1 sense cholesterol, and that in Niemann-Pick type C, a disease in which cholesterol is trapped in lysosomes, these contacts drive abnormal growth signalling. Lim also co-authored a 2017 Cancer Discovery study on drugs that target both the recycling and the growth-signalling roles of the lysosome.

PubMed now lists Lim at the School of Basic Medical Sciences of Guangzhou National Laboratory and Guangzhou Medical University. As senior author of a 2026 EMBO Journal paper, Lim reported that the lysosomal LAMTOR-Rag complex, the same docking station that recruits mTORC1, acts as a checkpoint for the production of the antiviral signal interferon-beta in macrophages. Lim also co-authored a 2025 structure of the KICSTOR and GATOR1-KICSTOR complexes, which hold an mTORC1 brake on the lysosome, with Ming-Yuan Su, another Berkeley alumnus in this Atlas.

story: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the immune system attacks myelin, the fatty insulation around nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord. Chandrayee Banerjee is first author of a 2026 review on how two signalling systems talk to each other in MS (BANERJEE2026). One is the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which controls growth and metabolism in immune cells and in the oligodendrocytes that make myelin. The other is JAK/STAT, which carries signals from inflammatory messengers into the cell nucleus. The review argues that the two pathways reinforce each other in driving Th17 inflammatory T cells and microglia, the brain's immune cells, and that mTOR has two faces in MS: it helps oligodendrocytes mature and rebuild myelin, but too much of it feeds damage. It is a review of earlier studies, not new experiments, and drugs that hit both pathways at once have not been tested in people with MS.

PubMed lists three 2026 papers with Banerjee, all from Sidharth Mehan's neuroscience group in the Department of Pharmacology at ISF College of Pharmacy in Moga. The other two are reviews on repurposing older drugs for brain disease: the antihistamine clemastine as a promoter of myelin repair, and the osteoporosis drug raloxifene as a possible neuroprotective agent. No institutional profile page was found, so the position shown is the one on these papers.

studies.title: Decoding the PI3K/Akt/mTOR-JAK/STAT signaling axis in multiple sclerosis: mechanistic crosstalk and therapeutic opportunities.

current.sub: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center and Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, and Texas A&M University College of Medicine (papers 2025–2026) · Texas A&M University (2022 paper) · Division of Cardiovascular Surgery, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (papers 2017–2021)
story: Samson Hennessy-Strahs is first author of an Atlas study (HEN2026) on alveolar macrophages, the immune cells that sit in the tiny air sacs of the lung and swallow up surfactant, the soapy film that keeps the sacs open. In mice, the team removed mTOR only from myeloid cells, the family that includes macrophages. The alveolar macrophages slowly disappeared, the ones left could not eat particles well, fat built up inside them, and the lungs filled with material in a pattern resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a rare human lung disease. Treating normal mice with the mTOR-blocking drug temsirolimus gave a similar picture.

The finding matters because mTOR inhibitors are used in transplant patients and in cancer, and some patients develop lung problems on them. The study suggests one possible reason: the drugs may starve the lung's own cleaning crew. The work was done in mice, so whether the same happens in patients still has to be shown.

The publication record shows two research phases. From 2017 to 2021 Hennessy-Strahs worked in the Division of Cardiovascular Surgery at the University of Pennsylvania, mostly with Carlo Bartoli, on how left ventricular assist devices (mechanical heart pumps) damage blood proteins such as von Willebrand factor and cause abnormal blood vessels in the gut. A 2022 paper lists Texas A&M University. Since 2025 the papers come from Xian C. current.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
current.role: Researcher in Jukka Hakkola's pharmacology group at the University of Oulu who led a clinical and mouse study showing that activating the drug sensor PXR makes the liver grow
current.sub: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Biocenter Oulu, University of Oulu and Oulu University Hospital (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2025 to 2026)
story: Piia Lassila is the first author of LASSILA2026. The study gave the antibiotic rifampicin, which strongly activates the liver's drug-sensing receptor PXR, to 16 healthy volunteers for a week, and measured liver size. The liver grew by about 2.7 percent relative to body weight. In male mice, activating PXR also enlarged the liver, and the growth came with more activity in the AKT-MTOR pathway, the cell's main growth-signalling route, without activation of the YAP pathway. This matters because many common medicines activate PXR, and it shows that such drugs can change the size of a human organ within days.

PubMed lists Lassila on two papers, both from Jukka Hakkola's group at the University of Oulu. In the other, from 2025, she was a co-author of the discovery that the cell-adhesion protein Lasp2 is a new PXR target gene in mouse liver.
No official profile was found, so training and current position beyond the University of Oulu affiliation are not given.

current.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
current.role: Cancer biologist in Anindya Bagchi's lab who found that a tiny protein made from the circular RNA circPVT1 keeps MYC levels high through mTORC1
current.sub: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, Anindya Bagchi lab (2026) · Masonic Cancer Center, University of Minnesota, and Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, Gurgaon, India (2014)
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Ashutosh Tiwari is first author of this study. The work continues a long collaboration with Anindya Bagchi: Tiwari is also a co-author of the 2014 Nature paper, from Bagchi's group at the University of Minnesota, which showed that cancers with extra MYC copies depend on PVT1. At that time PubMed listed Tiwari at the Masonic Cancer Center in Minneapolis and at the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute in Gurgaon, India.

In 2026, Tiwari was also a co-author of a second Genes and Development paper from the Bagchi lab, on Honeybadger, another micropeptide made from an alternative transcript, which holds back RAS-MAPK signalling. A formal title for Tiwari's current position could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Firefox, a protein encoded by circular PVT1, is essential for MYC-driven oncogenesis.

current.lab_name: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
current.role: Rheumatologist and researcher at the University of Tokyo who studies how B cells go wrong in lupus, and first author of the 2026 study tying the arginine sensor CASTOR1 to mTORC1 in antibody-making cells
current.sub: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (group of senior author Fujio, 2026) · Department of Medicine and Rheumatology, Tokyo Metropolitan Geriatric Hospital (2023) · Department of Rheumatology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (2016)
story: Cells check whether they have enough of each amino acid before they grow. CASTOR1 is a sensor for the amino acid arginine: when arginine is low, CASTOR1 holds mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in check. In the Atlas study KUS2026, Kusuda and colleagues in the University of Tokyo group of senior author Fujio gave CASTOR1 a clear job in the body. In mice without CASTOR1, mTORC1 was overactive in B cells, the immune cells that make antibodies. The mice made more plasma cells (antibody factories), more antibodies including ones against their own DNA, and developed kidney inflammation like that seen in lupus.

Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. In blood from people with lupus, plasmablasts with less CASTOR1 went with more active disease. That human result is a correlation; the cause-and-effect evidence comes from mice. The study is one of few that link a specific nutrient sensor upstream of mTORC1 to a human autoimmune disease.

PubMed shows Kusuda as a clinician as well as a researcher: a 2016 case report from the Department of Rheumatology at Tokyo Medical and Dental University, and a 2023 letter on COVID-19 vaccination and rheumatoid arthritis in older patients from the Tokyo Metropolitan Geriatric Hospital, with a joint affiliation at the University of Tokyo. Rank and training details could not be confirmed.

studies.title: CASTOR1 regulates humoral immune responses and contributes to the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus

current.lab_name: Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, Hubei University of Medicine (Xiangyang, China)
current.role: Cardiothoracic surgery researcher in Xiangyang who tests natural compounds against lung cancer cells, including gambogic acid acting on the AKT and mTOR pathway
current.sub: Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, affiliated with Hubei University of Medicine (papers 2021–2026)
story: Su Bo is first author of the Atlas study BO2026, which tested gambogic acid, a yellow compound from the resin of the gamboge tree, on lung cancer cells. The study had two parts. In the computer part, network pharmacology and molecular docking (a simulation of how well a molecule fits into a protein) suggested that gambogic acid binds most tightly to AKT and to S6K1, a kinase that mTORC1 switches on to drive growth. In the lab part, the compound killed A549 lung cancer cells and pushed them into apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death.

The study did not measure whether gambogic acid directly blocks the mTOR enzyme, and it had no animal or human data. Docking predicts possible binding but does not prove it, so the link to mTOR remains a hypothesis to test.

PubMed lists Bo at the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery of Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, a hospital of Hubei University of Medicine. An earlier paper from the same department (2021) followed the same approach with purpurin, another plant-derived compound, which killed A549 lung cancer cells through oxidative stress and lower PI3K/AKT signalling. No official profile page was found.

studies.title: Molecular and metabolic dysregulation of lung cancer in developing anti-tumor activity by gambogic acid mediated mTOR signaling: in vitro and computational study.

current.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
current.role: Hematology researcher in Hangzhou who studies treatment of bone-marrow failure, including the use of sirolimus (rapamycin) in pure red cell aplasia
current.sub: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Zhejiang Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine) and The First School of Clinical Medicine, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (papers 2026)
story: In pure red cell aplasia, the bone marrow stops making red blood cells while white cells and platelets are spared. The acquired form is often driven by the immune system, so it is treated with immune-suppressing drugs such as ciclosporin. In SUN2026, Zexing Sun and colleagues in Dijiong Wu's group looked back at patients treated at one hospital whose disease had not responded to ciclosporin and who then received sirolimus, the drug also called rapamycin, which blocks mTOR in immune cells. 54.5 percent responded, and 64.3 percent of those whose aplasia was secondary to another disease. Responses did not depend on mutations in STAT3 or STAT5B, genes often altered in the abnormal lymphocytes linked to this disease. The study was retrospective, at one centre, with no randomised control group, so it cannot prove that sirolimus works better than ciclosporin.

Sun works in the Department of Hematology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University in Hangzhou. In 2026 the same group also published a single-centre comparison of stem cell transplant donor types in aplastic anaemia, on which Sun was a co-author. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Favorable response to second-line sirolimus regardless of STAT3/5b status in acquired pure red cell aplasia: A retrospective study from a single center.

current.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
current.role: Kidney researcher at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, and first author of a 2026 study tracing a chain of enzymes that switches on mTOR and drives scarring in damaged kidneys
current.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Chronic kidney disease often ends in fibrosis, a slow scarring in which working kidney tissue is replaced by stiff connective tissue. In the 2026 study led by Shiqi Lv, with Xiaoyan Zhang as senior author, the team followed a chain of four molecules. USP7 is a deubiquitinase, an enzyme that removes ubiquitin tags, the labels that send proteins to be destroyed. By removing them from KDM5B, USP7 keeps KDM5B stable. KDM5B is a histone demethylase, an enzyme that strips activating marks from the proteins that package DNA, and here it silences the gene for TSC1. TSC1 is part of the brake on mTOR, so less TSC1 means more mTOR activity and more scarring.

The evidence comes from two mouse models of kidney injury, where blocking USP7 genetically or with a drug restored TSC1, damped mTOR and reduced fibrosis, and from human kidney samples, where USP7 levels were higher in chronic kidney disease and tracked with how much scarring was present. The human part is a correlation; the cause-and-effect steps were shown in mice and cells.

PubMed lists Shiqi Lv at the Department of Nephrology of Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, in Shanghai. No official profile page could be checked, so the current position is given as at the time of the study.

studies.title: Deubiquitinase USP7 stabilizes the histone demethylase KDM5B and promotes the progression of renal fibrosis through the TSC1/mTOR axis

current.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
current.role: Researcher in the orthopedics department of Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 study on corilagin, a plant polyphenol that protected mouse cartilage by restoring autophagy
current.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Ruijia Zhou's 2026 study, with Hongbo You as senior author, looked for a way to protect cartilage in osteoarthritis. Cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, need autophagy to clear damaged parts, and too much PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling holds autophagy back. Inflammation driven by NF-kappaB adds to the damage.

Corilagin, a polyphenol from several medicinal plants, damped both PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB in chondrocytes. Autophagy recovered and the cells produced more extracellular matrix, the tough material of cartilage. In mice whose knee joints were destabilised surgically (the DMM model), corilagin reduced cartilage erosion and joint damage scores. The results come from cells and mice only.

PubMed lists Ruijia Zhou at the Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

studies.title: Corilagin attenuates osteoarthritis progression by coordinating NF-κB inhibition with PI3K/AKT/mTOR-associated autophagy restoration.

current.lab_name: Lin Lab, Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health, University of Missouri (Columbia, Missouri, USA)
current.role: Researcher in Ai-Ling Lin's group at the University of Missouri who studies how rapamycin and the gut microbiome affect brain blood flow and metabolism in people and mice at genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease
current.sub: Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health, University of Missouri (Ai-Ling Lin lab, papers 2024–2026)
story: APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Carriers often show lower blood flow and weaker energy use in the brain years before any memory problems. In the Atlas study AWARE2026, Chetan Aware was first author of a small pilot trial at the University of Missouri. Twenty-three cognitively normal adults aged 45 to 65 took 1 mg of rapamycin a day for four weeks. In the nine APOE4 carriers, blood flow in several brain regions rose by more than 15%, while non-carriers showed no clear change. Blood markers of metabolism and inflammation improved, and the gut microbiome shifted. There was no placebo group and very few participants, so this is early evidence that needs a controlled trial.

Aware works in Ai-Ling Lin's group in the Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health at the University of Missouri. The group had earlier shown in mice carrying human APOE4 that 16 weeks of rapamycin improved mitochondrial function and nerve-cell signalling in the brain, with different effects in APOE3 mice; Aware was a co-author of that 2024 study. In 2026 Aware was first author of a mouse study in which gut bacteria taken from stroke patients sped up tau changes and brain inflammation in Alzheimer's model mice, pointing to the gut-brain connection as a possible link between stroke and later dementia. No official profile page was found.

studies.title: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial.

current.lab_name: Do-Hyung Kim Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
current.role: Autophagy researcher in Do-Hyung Kim's University of Minnesota lab who mapped how the kinase ULK1 starts autophagy, and lead author of work showing that AMPK can hold ULK1 back under energy stress
current.sub: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (papers with Do-Hyung Kim, 2013–2023)
story: Ji-Man Park is the first author of PAR2023, a Nature Communications paper from Do-Hyung Kim's lab at the University of Minnesota. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane and breaks them down. The kinase ULK1 starts the process. A textbook model said that AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, switches ULK1 on when energy runs low. In cultured cells starved of glucose or with poisoned mitochondria, the team found the opposite: AMPK held ULK1 and autophagy back. AMPK also shielded the ULK1 machinery from being cut up by caspases, enzymes active in cell death, so autophagy could restart later. This challenges a common reading of how energy stress and autophagy are linked, though it comes from cell culture.

Park's PubMed record shows a long run of ULK1 work in the same lab. As first author, Park showed in 2016 that ULK1 binds and phosphorylates ATG14, a step that passes the mTORC1 signal on to the autophagy machinery, and in 2018 that ULK1 phosphorylates BECN1 (Beclin 1) on serine 30 to drive autophagy. Park also contributed to the lab's 2014 Molecular Cell paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG to slow autophagosome maturation, and co-wrote a 2023 commentary in Autophagy titled "A paradigm shift: AMPK negatively regulates ULK1 activity".
All of these papers list the University of Minnesota. No official profile page was found, so the current position could not be confirmed; the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Redefining the role of AMPK in autophagy and the energy stress response
